title: Greedy Best-First: Fastest Path in Tallinn Streets!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race through a real street-map graph, always expanding the node that looks closest to the goal. It’s thrillingly quick—and sometimes “too sure”—showing how heuristics shape pathfinding behavior.
ig_caption:
🧭⚡ **Greedy Best-First in Tallinn (Kristiine)**

In this visualization, we treat the street network as a **graph** (intersections = nodes, roads = edges). Greedy Best-First uses a **priority queue** and ranks frontier nodes purely by a **heuristic estimate** h(n) of distance to the goal—typically something like **straight-line distance** on coordinates.

📌 **Key idea (graph theory):** the algorithm selects the next node with the smallest h(n), so it **doesn’t necessarily minimize total path cost (g)**—it minimizes *estimated distance-to-go*. That’s why you may see it dart toward the destination quickly, yet occasionally miss a shorter route.

🧠 Each expansion step is a lesson in heuristic-driven **best-first graph search**: how the heuristic steers exploration, how the frontier changes, and why admissibility/consistency matter (Greedy ≠ A*).

🚦 **Greedy Best-First on a real street graph (Tallinn - Kristiine)!**

We convert roads into a graph (nodes and edges), then run **Greedy Best-First search**, which always expands the next intersection that *looks* closest to the goal using a heuristic distance. It’s a fast, heuristic-driven pathfinding method that’s great for demonstrating how graph search decisions are made—share your thoughts and hit follow for more algorithm visuals!
